topic: Digital tools and cognitive offloading: remembering the content, or remembering where to find it
scope: A narrative review of fixed source summaries, not a systematic review; the summaries below were written by the project authors and are not quotations from the originals.

S1.title: Google effects on memory: cognitive consequences of having information at our fingertips
S1.authors: Betsy Sparrow; Jenny Liu; Daniel M. Wegner
S1.summary: The abstract summarizes four studies: when people expect to have future access to information, they recall the information itself less well and recall better where to find it.
S1.limit: The given summary says nothing about long-term classroom learning and does not involve modern generative AI; it does not show that the internet permanently lowers everyone's memory.

S2.title: Cognitive Offloading
S2.authors: Evan F. Risko; Sam J. Gilbert
S2.summary: Handing part of information processing to the environment or to tools in order to reduce the cognitive demands of a task is cognitive offloading. The review discusses what triggers offloading and its cognitive consequences, and proposes a metacognitive framework connecting results from several fields.
S2.limit: This is a review framework, not a single intervention trial; the concept itself does not prove that any particular tool necessarily improves or harms learning.

S3.title: Guidance for generative AI in education and research
S3.summary: The guidance argues for a human-centred use of generative AI, protecting privacy, and having educational institutions validate tools for educational suitability. It discusses teaching design and research use and emphasizes human agency.
S3.limit: Policy guidance is not an experimental result showing learning effects; linking it to cognitive offloading is the author's own analytical inference and must be stated as such.
